title: GCSE Results: 9 Surprising Findings in 2026
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles uses the newly released 2026 GCSE data to argue that English, uniquely among subjects, is stagnating or declining while maths and other knowledge-heavy subjects improve, and he pins the blame on a curriculum culture that has never fully embraced retrieval practice. He extends this into a wider critique of academisation (arguing centralised MAT control has ironically killed the competitive experimentation that free schools and, oddly, under-resourced local authorities now outperform), of AQA's exam and mark-scheme design as structurally punitive to top English students, and of a job market and AI-driven subject-choice shift (toward statistics, business, and sociology, away from engineering and computing) that he reads as evidence schools have lost sight of education's intrinsic purpose. He closes with a speculative but data-anchored observation that boys are narrowing the gender attainment gap, which he attributes tentatively to a reactive backlash against manosphere rhetoric that is nonetheless motivating some boys to re-engage with school. Throughout, the piece moves rapidly between hard exam statistics and provocative interpretive claims, in Salles's characteristic contrarian newsletter voice.
points: English's stagnant National Reference Test results, contrasted with maths' adjusted grade boundaries, is read as direct evidence that inconsistent, ad hoc retrieval practice in English departments (versus systematic use of platforms like Sparx Maths) explains the subject's comparative decline.

Salles argues academisation has paradoxically destroyed the 'free market' school-improvement mechanism Gove intended, because MATs centralise control the way local authorities once did, while genuinely autonomous Free schools and now-underfunded local-authority schools outperform them.

He attributes roughly 80% of English GCSE entries' grade outcomes to AQA specifically, framing the exam board's mark schemes and question design as structurally biased against top students regardless of their reading history or ability.

Subject-entry shifts toward statistics, business, and sociology and away from engineering and computing are interpreted as students hedging against AI-driven and economic job-market uncertainty rather than pursuing subjects for intrinsic enjoyment.

The narrowing gender attainment gap is tentatively explained as a reactive effect of 'manosphere' rhetoric: boys not persuaded by figures like Andrew Tate but 'uplifted by the change in the zeitgeist' to work harder against a less forgiving environment.
quotes: Results at grade 7 are not statistically significantly different to 2017. At grade 4, there is an indication that attainment has fallen since 2017.
With Free schools, this has been a spectacular success. They out perform local authority schools and academies.
Trusts are build on centralised control - they've become the cumbersome beasts that used to be local authorities, and so they achieve less well.
It isn't rocket science, it is cognitive science. Here's another irony for you. English literature is a 90% fact based subject.
9 years of AQA, who dominate the English GCSE market, has perpetuated damaging myths about their exam, so that teachers are focusing on the wrong skills.
About 80% of English entries are AQA. They determine who gets what grades. And the structure of AQA exams and marking criteria force students to do worse in English than other subjects.
We have lost the soul of education. Study is simply a way to get grades, and we motivate students to get grades by dangling the idea of career success.

Andrew Tate and his ilk peddle their offensive, even violent sexist diatribe about male and female roles, and the gullible are taken in. But, in the wake of that are boys who are not sucked in by the misogyny, but are uplifted by the change in the zeitgeist.
